extracted.intended_audience: American newspaper readers and policymakers (19th-century readers of political dispatches)
extracted.subtask_description: First‑person letters and news dispatches reporting military, diplomatic, and civic events in revolutionary Rome, aimed at informing and persuading a foreign public and policymakers. Emphasizes factual reporting, moral judgment, and prescriptions for diplomatic conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of governments chosen by the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The only dignified ground for our government... is to recognize for any nation the government chosen by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize a nation's government so long as it can sustain itself; legitimacy derives from self‑chosen authority and correct suffrage. The writer argues America is bound to recognize the Roman government while it can sustain itself, regardless of other nations' views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral diplomatic support (recognition as moral strength)
rubrics_metrics.description: Had Mr. Cass been empowered to act as Mr. Rush did in France, [he] might have morally strengthened the staggering republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diplomatic acknowledgment and moral encouragement can strengthen fledgling republics even if material support fails; acting on principle is preferable to withholding recognition out of fear of consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Envoy conduct must not signal disbelief in local government
rubrics_metrics.description: When all the other ambassadors are at Gaëta, ours is in Rome, as if by his presence to discountenance the republican government, which he does not recognize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An envoy's presence or posture should not publicly imply lack of confidence in a local government; diplomatic positioning can wound local pride and affect popular sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship cannot be imposed by violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship and violence are incompatible. Thus it would be inconsistent on our part to begin by firing our cannon upon you, since we are your natural protectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A protecting power that uses force undermines any claim of friendship; coercion is incompatible with genuine protective/amicable relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign powers must choose: recognize, oppose, or be sincere neutral
rubrics_metrics.description: There are for France only three parts to take in the Roman States. She ought to declare herself for us, against us, or neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Half‑measures (occupation under pretext of protection) are unacceptable. If neutral, neutrality must be sincere; if for or against, act clearly. Occupation or undeclared intervention creates distrust and grave consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect conventions and armistices until ratified or declined
rubrics_metrics.description: The Assembly... having concluded a convention from the 31st of May, 1849, with M. de Lesseps... must consider that convention obligatory for both parties, and indeed a safeguard of the rights of nations, until it has been ratified or declined by the government of France.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreements made in the field or by plenipotentiaries should be honored until the sending government explicitly ratifies or rejects them; unilateral hostile acts during the interim violate rights of nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign military occupation undermines broader defense and invites enemy gains
rubrics_metrics.description: Your forces are disposed around our walls as if for a siege. They remain there without avowed aim... They have forced us to keep the city in a state of defence which weighs upon our finances. They force us to keep here a body of troops who might be saving our cities from the occupation and ravages of the Austrians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interventions that concentrate local defensive forces inward leave frontiers and allied regions exposed; planners should consider strategic spillover effects of 'protective' occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign powers should not detain arms or obstruct aid
rubrics_metrics.description: We had bought in France arms for our defence. Of these ten thousand muskets have been detained between Marseilles and Civita Vecchia. These are in your hands. Thus with a single blow you deprive us of ten thousand soldiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect delivery of purchased arms and avoid naval/cruiser actions that prevent other states or volunteers from bringing aid; withholding arms is a material interference with a people's ability to defend themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombardment or destruction of cultural and civic heritage
rubrics_metrics.description: Rome, precious inheritance of mankind,--will they run the risk of marring her shrined treasures?... The cannonade reverberates all day under the dome of St. Peter's...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military actions which risk irreparable damage to universal cultural monuments and civilian patrimony are morally and politically fraught and should be avoided whenever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain factual reporting over personal feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain facts are the best; for my feelings I could not find fit words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting on grave political/military events, prioritize concrete facts and observable events rather than extended personal sentiment to best inform readers and influence policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of partisan or foreign‑influenced press accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists not in Europe a paper more violently opposed to the cause of freedom than the Times, and neither its leaders nor its foreign correspondence are to be depended upon. It is said to receive money from Austria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess newspapers' reliability critically; reports may be colored by political sympathies or external financing, so corroboration and skepticism are warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupation risks civil war and destroys effective self‑government
rubrics_metrics.description: They foresee, the troops being once admitted, changes in men and in actions which would be fatal to their liberty. They know that, in presence of foreign bayonets, the independence of their Assembly, of their government, would be a vain word. They have always Civita Vecchia before their eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that foreign troops within a capital can nullify domestic institutions and provoke internal collapse or civil conflict; occupation has severe political costs beyond immediate military considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral duty to resist external imposition to preserve sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: To resist,--we owed this to our country, to France, to all Europe. We ought... maintain to our country the inviolability, so far as that was possible to us, of its territory, and of the institutions...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A government and people may be justified in resisting externally imposed compromises or interventions to defend territorial integrity and the self‑determination of their institutions.
